title: Will the Nationwide Ground Stop Affect Your Thanksgiving Travel Plans?
author: Chantelle Lee
body:
Nearly 6 million people are expected to fly within the U.S. over the Thanksgiving holiday, just a little more than a week after a telecommunications issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to order a nationwide ground stop that continued to disrupt flights around the country even days after it ended.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the FAA issued the nationwide ground stop after router upgrade work led to a series of communication breakdowns.

The incident led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays throughout the weekend. On Saturday alone, 6,700 flights within, into, or out of the U.S. were canceled, according to the flight-tracking website FlightAware. The following day saw another 2,336 cancellations.

The days of flight disruptions have left many wondering if Friday’s incident could cascade into next week, when 5.96 million people are set to travel by air for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to AAA’s projections.

But on Tuesday, the FAA said that it had temporarily halted installing routers tied to Friday's issue. And experts say that the country’s air travel system has mostly recovered from the ground stop, and that they don’t anticipate Friday’s disruption to impact holiday travel.

The number of U.S. flight cancellations dropped from the thousands per day experienced over the weekend to about 375 on Monday. As of Tuesday evening, FlightAware reported only 91 flight cancellations within, into, or out of the U.S.

Will the nationwide ground stop affect my Thanksgiving travel plans?

Daniel Bubb, a commercial aviation historian and former airline pilot and professor in residence at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, says that it typically takes one to four days for the air travel system to recover after a disruption like this, so any lingering effects from Friday’s incident will likely subside well before the holiday long weekend.

“You may see a little bit of delay, a little bit more cancellation [right now], but not as bad as it was over the weekend,” Bubb says. “We’re mostly recovered.”

Sheldon Jacobson, an aviation security and safety expert and professor of computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, says that, on an average day, as many as 250 commercial flights may be canceled in the U.S. so the latest numbers suggest that the air travel system has recovered and is “back to [a] steady state in terms of operations.”

What may last throughout the holiday, Jacobson says, is people’s anxiety about air travel. He says that the nationwide ground stop may have left some people feeling wary of the country’s air travel system.

“What we have not returned to is trust because people are thinking ‘Okay, this happened once, it was unexpected, can it happen again?’” Jacobson says.

While he and Bubb both urge the government to upgrade and strengthen the country’s air travel system in a bipartisan way, they also assure the public that the U.S. air travel system is safe.

“People should take comfort in knowing that our air traffic system is safe,” Bubb says. “It’s fundamentally sound and safe, but it’s not helpful when you have these disruptions.”

What steps can I take to make my Thanksgiving air travel go smoothly?

The Thanksgiving holiday is one of the busiest travel periods of the year, Bubb says. He adds that if there’s inclement weather, people may face flight delays and even cancellations.

It’s good practice to keep up-to-date on the status of your flight by signing up for alerts with your airline. If your flight is canceled, contact your airline’s customer service to rebook your flight.

Jacobson also recommends that people pack appropriately to make their experience at the airport as smooth as possible. For instance, he suggests that if someone is bringing a holiday gift, they should bring the wrapping paper with them but pack the gift unwrapped because if airport security flags the item for additional screening, the agents may have to unwrap a wrapped gift. Jacobson also advises that people check their bags before they begin packing to make sure that nothing was left behind from a previous trip.

“Little things like that go a long way in making people’s plans a little smoother,” Jacobson says.

Both Jacobson and Bubb also encourage people to be patient and kind to airport and airline staff during their travels next week.

“Remember: the people who are working for the airlines on Thanksgiving and on Christmas, they are giving up their holiday so that you can travel to enjoy your holiday,” Jacobson says. “Kindness is free to give, and it makes tremendous dividends for all.”
